query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The ability of HEA nanoparticles to maintain a single, chemically homogeneous solid solution at high operating temperatures (473–1923 K) is controlled by a synergy between high configurational entropy and lattice distortion effects. Specifically, a significant atomic size mismatch (lattice distortion) reduces atomic diffusivity, which, coupled with the stabilizing high mixing entropy, suppresses phase segregation and chemical ordering even under high thermal energy input by inducing sluggish diffusion.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near‐equiatomic ratios, initially crystallized as a single-phase solid solution at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Expose the HEA nanoparticles to a controlled thermal program ramping from 473 K to 1923 K under catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted in an inert or relevant catalytic atmosphere with controlled heating/cooling rates, ensuring that particle size, support interactions, and synthesis history are maintained constant; temperatures spanning from 473 K up to 1923 K.
generation.structural_mediator: The intrinsic lattice distortion induced by atomic size mismatch in combination with high configurational entropy.
generation.mechanism: High mixing entropy favors the disordered solid solution, while lattice distortion reduces atomic mobility thereby inducing sluggish diffusion; this dual effect counteracts thermally driven phase segregation or ordering during high-temperature operation, preserving both the structural and chemical homogeneity required for optimal catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEA nanoparticles with a significant degree of lattice distortion will retain their single-phase structure and uniform elemental distribution at high temperatures (up to 1923 K) and will continue to exhibit high catalytic activity and thermoelectric performance. In contrast, nanoparticles with lower lattice distortion (i.e., smaller atomic size mismatch) may show signs of phase separation or chemical segregation under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: The initial room-temperature, single-phase solid solution state of the HEA nanoparticles with uniform elemental distribution.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for nanoparticles synthesized to be homogeneous and near equiatomic in composition, and under controlled thermal ramping without extreme external perturbations. Variations in synthesis method or unintentional doping may lead to deviations from the predicted behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative influence of lattice distortion on atomic diffusivity and the critical threshold of atomic size mismatch necessary to suppress phase segregation under ultrahigh temperatures remains to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of HEA nanoparticles: one designed with a high degree of atomic size variance (and thus greater lattice distortion) and one with a reduced size variance (less lattice distortion), while keeping mixing entropy similar. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature treatments up to 1923 K under catalytic/thermoelectric conditions. Perform in situ TEM imaging, EDS mapping, and XRD analysis during and after the heat treatment.
measurements: In situ TEM for morphological evolution and phase homogeneity
Catalytic activity and thermoelectric performance tests before and after heating
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA nanoparticles with higher lattice distortion (high atomic size variance) do not maintain a chemically homogeneous single-phase structure—evidenced by observable phase segregation, chemical ordering, or degradation in catalytic/thermoelectric performance relative to the baseline—or if both sets behave equivalently regardless of lattice distortion differences, then the hypothesis is falsified.

In contrast to conventional alloy materials based on single principal elements, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have recently received considerable attention in various fields because of their unique physical and chemical properties. In principle, HEAs are produced by alloying five or more metal elements in nearly equal proportions (recently extended to 5 to 35 at%) into solid solutions with a high mixing entropy rather than an intermetallic phase. The resulting synergistic effect endows HEAs with high mechanical strength, good thermal stability, and catalytic activity. In particularly, HEAs displayed appraisable catalytic performance in electrocatalytic water splitting, ammonia oxidation and decomposition, and CO2 reduction. Mechanistic studies suggest that the ligand effect and distortion effect of HEAs, which arise from tuning the composition and geometric properties of HEAs to a large degree, could significantly modify the electronic properties of active sites and consequently improve their catalytic performance. The inherent synergy effect of HEAs provides possibility to boost the catalytic activity by combining suitable metals.
